subject: General Science
title: The Solar System — Sun, Planets, Asteroids & Comets (concept)
journey: Where does Earth live and who lives next door? (hook) → Cosmic Creations — model the solar system (investigate)
coming_up: Is the Moon a shape-shifter? (hook) → Modelling the Moon's Phases (investigate)

outcome.text: The solar system is the Sun and everything held by its gravity — eight planets in their orbits, plus asteroids and comets — with distance from the Sun alone NOT deciding how hot a planet is.

prepare: yesterday's stones/pebbles used to model the asteroid belt (kept, or the teacher's own memory of the activity, to point back to)

keywords.meaning: a family of planets, moons and other space objects that all orbit — go around — one star, held together by that star's pulling force (gravity).
the curved path one space object follows as it travels around another, larger object, again and again.
a rocky chunk, smaller than a planet, that orbits the Sun — many of them travel together in a wide band called the asteroid belt.
a ball of ice, dust and frozen gas that orbits the Sun; when it passes close to the Sun, its ice starts to melt and it grows a long, glowing tail.
the four rocky planets that orbit closest to the Sun.
the planets that orbit farther from the Sun, most of them huge and made mostly of gas.

blocks.text: Fatima wonders aloud: which planet do YOU think is the HOTTEST in our whole solar system — the one closest to the Sun, or a different one? And where does Bilal think Earth sits in the line-up of planets? Write your two guesses in your notebook now, and one reason for each, before we check together.

blocks.label: On the page · read aloud
lines: Fatima: “Which planet do you think is the HOTTEST — the closest one, or a different one?”

blocks.instruction: Reveal the hook's answer: Mercury is closest to the Sun but has no atmosphere to trap heat, so it cools quickly at night. Venus, though further away, has a thick atmosphere that traps heat like a blanket — making it the HOTTEST planet, hotter than Mercury. Earth sits third from the Sun, among the four rocky Inner Planets, held in its orbit by the Sun's gravity.
script: Distance alone does not decide the heat — Venus proves it.
Mercury is closer but bare; Venus is further but wrapped in a heat-trapping blanket of air.
That blanket is the whole reason.
blocks.instruction2: Fill in the board's two columns together: INNER PLANETS (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars — rocky, closer to the Sun) and OUTER PLANETS (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune — mostly gas, farther out). Explain: gravity from the Sun holds every one of them in its orbit, like a family held together by its parent.
script2: Everything in this family — planets, moons, asteroids, comets — is held by the Sun's own gravity, the way a parent holds a family together.

steps: Two OUTER planets, a different pair from the ones we already named. Saturn is the second-largest planet and, like Jupiter, a gas giant with no solid surface — but Saturn is so light for its size that, if there were an ocean big enough, it would actually FLOAT on water. It also carries a stunning collection of icy, rocky rings. Neptune, the farthest sibling of all, is dark, cold and constantly stormy — and because it orbits so far from the Sun, it takes a huge 165 Earth years just to complete ONE full circle. Same solar-system family as Mercury and Venus, a different, much farther-out pair of siblings. (Grounded in p.189's own Saturn/Neptune facts.)

blocks.text: Explain in your own words: is a comet more like a planet, an asteroid, or something different from both? Use today's definitions.
Halfway check · minute 17. By now the class should be starting WE DO.

lines: Turn-and-talk during We-Do's asteroid-vs-comet comparison (2-minute exchange per pair, then report to the class).
circulate; for a pair stuck on the difference, ask 'which one is made of ice, and which one is solid rock?'

blocks.instruction: In pairs, recall yesterday's asteroid-belt model (the rocks placed between Mars and Jupiter) and connect it to today's NEW term, comet. Model with one pair leading: Zainab names what the class's rocks stood for while Ahmed reasons out loud how a comet is different, then all pairs compare asteroids and comets using the board's keyWords definitions.
script: Yesterday's rocks were asteroids — rocky chunks orbiting in a belt.
Today's new object is icy: a comet, which only grows its bright tail once it gets close enough to the Sun for its ice to start melting.

lines: میرے خیال میں سیارچے اور دُم دار ستارے میں فرق یہ ہے کہ ... (I think the difference between an asteroid and a comet is ...)
کیونکہ صفحہ 190 پر لِکھا ہے کہ ... (Because page 190 says ...)
Independently answer Skill Sharpener Q2, Q3 and Q5 (p.191), using today's Inner/Outer Planets board list and the solar-system family idea.
blocks.say: You have the board's two planet groups and today's family idea. Use them on your own now, working alone before we check together.

items.q: Skill Sharpener Q1 (p.191): Which planet is closest to the Sun? A) Mars B) Earth C) Saturn D) Mercury
items.answer: D) Mercury — the innermost planet, closest to the Sun, as named on p.188.

items.q: Skill Sharpener Q2 (p.191): Which planet has the Giant Red Spot? A) Mars B) Jupiter C) Venus D) Saturn
items.answer: B) Jupiter — its massive storms are visible through space, and one of them is called the Giant Red Spot (p.189).

items.q: Skill Sharpener Q3 (p.191): Name the four inner planets.
items.answer: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars — the four rocky planets closest to the Sun (p.188).

items.q: Skill Sharpener Q4 (p.191): If the Sun's light suddenly vanished, how long would it take for you to notice?
items.answer: About 8 minutes — sunlight takes roughly 8 minutes to travel the 150,000,000 km from the Sun to Earth (p.188).

items.q: Skill Sharpener Q5 (p.191): How is Earth optimal for life?
items.answer: Earth has water, breathable air, an ozone layer that protects us from the Sun's harmful rays, and a Moon — this combination makes it the only known planet supporting life (p.189).

blocks.stuck: If a child cannot yet sort Inner vs Outer planets, drop to a smaller two-item ladder first: 'Mercury or Jupiter — which is small and rocky, which is huge and gassy?' before sorting the full eight.
blocks.early: Pluto used to be called the ninth planet, but scientists now call it a Dwarf Planet because of its small size (p.190 Fun Facts). Using today's Inner/Outer Planets idea, explain why size matters for how we group space objects.

items.q: Skill Sharpener Q4 (p.191): If the Sun's light suddenly vanished, how long would it take for you to notice, and why does it take that long at all?
items.criterion: Correct if the student says about 8 minutes AND explains that light takes time to travel the huge distance (150,000,000 km) from the Sun to Earth.

lines: Skill Sharpener Q1 (p.191) — which planet is closest to the Sun? Write the answer and one reason using today's Inner Planets idea.

coaching.ask_yourself: Watch for children who think 'closer to the Sun always means hotter' — Venus is today's counter-example, and the atmosphere reasoning is the real target, not just the fact itself.
